items.text: Is your coffee hot enough? ; This box isn't big enough.
He didn't work hard enough.

blocks.text: Rule 240
'Enough' is often followed by 'to' + infinitive.

items.text: He didn't work hard enough to pass the exam.
Is your coffee hot enough to drink?
She's not old enough to get married.

blocks.text: Rule 241
'Enough' can also be followed by 'for someone' or 'for something'.

items.text: The dress was big enough for me.
She's not experienced enough for this job.
He didn't work hard enough for a promotion.

blocks.text: Rule 242
'Enough' as a determiner meaning 'as much/many as necessary' goes before the noun it modifies. It is used with a countable noun in the plural and with an uncountable noun.

items.text: We have enough bread.
They don't have enough food.
We have enough pens.

blocks.text: Rule 243
To modify a verb, an adjective or another adverb, we use an adverb.

items.text: She writes very carefully. — It is wrong to say – She writes very careful. 'Careful' is an adjective which cannot modify the adverb 'very'. Therefore, 'carefully' (adverb) must be used in place of adjective 'careful'.

blocks.text: Rule 244
'Much' is used before a past participle and an adjective or adverb of a comparative degree; and 'very' is used before the present participle, and an adjective and an adverb of a positive degree.

items.text: The news is very surprising. — It is wrong to say – The news is much surprising.
I was much surprised at hearing the news. — It is wrong to say – I was very surprised at hearing the news.

blocks.text: Rule 245
'Much' is used with an uncountable noun and 'more' with a countable noun. There is no connection between much and more with the comparative and superlative.

items.text: I have much interest in cooking.
I have more friends to help me in problems.

blocks.text: Rule 246

Adjectives with two syllables can form the comparative either by adding -er or by preceding the adjective with 'more'. These adjectives form the superlative either by adding -est or by preceding the adjective with 'most'. In many cases, both forms are used, although one usage will be more common than the other. If you are not sure whether a two-syllable adjective can take a comparative or superlative ending, use 'more' and 'most' instead. For adjectives ending in y, change the y to an i before adding the ending.

items.text: Adjective — Comparative — Superlative
tilted — more tilted — most tilted
tangled — more tangled — most tangled
Adjective — Comparative — Superlative
important — more important — most important
expansive — more expansive — most expansive
adequate — more adequate — most adequate

blocks.text: Adjectives with three or more syllables form the comparative by putting 'more' in front of the adjective, and the superlative by putting 'most' in front.
Rule 247
'Too' is always an adverb, but it has two distinct meanings, each with its own usage patterns. Too as an adverb meaning 'also' goes at the end of the phrase it modifies.

items.text: I would like to go swimming too, if you will let me come.
Is this gift for me too?

blocks.text: Rule 248
Too as an adverb meaning 'excessively' goes before the adjective or adverb it modifies. It can be used in both affirmative and negative sentences.

items.text: He works too hard; Isn't she too young?

blocks.text: Rule 249
Too is often followed by 'to' + the infinitive.

items.text: The coffee was too hot to drink.
I am not too tired to go out tonight.
Don't you work too hard to have any free time?

blocks.text: Rule 250
'Too' can also be followed by 'for someone' or 'for something'.

items.text: The coffee was too hot for me.
The dress was too small for her.
He's not too old for this job.

blocks.text: Rule 251
'Ago' is always used with Past Indefinite tense. Therefore, if 'ago' is used in a sentence, that sentence must be in the Past Indefinite tense.

items.text: He came a month ago. — It is wrong to say – He has come a month ago.

blocks.text: Rule 252
'At present' means 'at this moment' and it is used with Present tense; whereas 'presently' and 'shortly' are used for referring to future action and generally used with Future Indefinite tense.

items.text: At present he is in the room. — It is wrong to say – Presently he is in the room.

blocks.text: Rule 253
'Early' means 'just after the beginning of anything' and 'soon' means 'just after a point of time'.

items.text: Roses blossomed early this spring.
The firing at the Line of Control started soon after midnight.

blocks.text: Rule 254
The sentence which starts with 'seldom', 'never', 'hardly', 'rarely' or 'scarcely' takes an inverse structure, i.e. Verb + Subject structure.

items.text: Seldom had I seen such a beautiful sight. — It is wrong to say – Seldom I had seen such a beautiful sight.

blocks.text: Rule 255
Inversion is also used in a sentence which starts with here / there / away / out / up / indoor or outdoor and main verb, or Aux. + Main Verb is used before the subject.

items.text: Away went Sita. — It is wrong to say – Away Sita went.

blocks.text: Rule 256
'A few' (for a countable noun) and 'a little' (for an uncountable noun) describe the quantity in a positive way, implying that although the speaker may not have much, he has enough.

items.text: I've got a few friends. = I have enough friends.
I have a few flowers in my garden. = I have enough flowers.
I've got a little money. = I have enough money.
I have a little free time on Thursdays. = I have enough free time.
Few people visited him in hospital. = He had almost no visitors, or perhaps no visitors at all.
I've seen few birds around here. = There are almost no birds, or perhaps not a single bird.
He had little money for treats. = Almost no money, or perhaps no money at all.
I have little time for TV = Almost no time, or perhaps no time at all.

blocks.text: 'Few' (for a countable noun) and 'little' (for an uncountable noun) describe the quantity in a negative way. They may actually indicate a total lack of the noun, but are more polite than saying so directly.
Rule 257
A preposition must always be followed by a noun or pronoun. That noun is called the object of the preposition. A verb can't be the object of a preposition.

items.text: The bone was for the dog. (Here, the preposition for is followed by the noun 'dog').
But, if we say – The bone was for walked. – This is not correct. The preposition for is followed by a verb 'walked', which can't be the object of a preposition.

blocks.text: Rule 258
As a preposition must always be followed by a noun and should have an object, it usually shouldn't be used at the end of a sentence.

items.text: The table is where I put my books on. — It is a wrong usage. Here, the use of the preposition 'on' isn't necessary. We could take the 'on' out of the sentence and the meaning would be the same.

But, if you say – 'I turned the TV on.' — It is correct. Here, if you remove the 'on' from the end of the sentence, it would change the meaning. Instead of switching on the set, you would be saying that you turned the TV itself.

blocks.text: Rule 259
Preposition 'to' is used for showing the person or thing that receives something.

items.text: He gave it to his sister
Who did she address the letter to ?
I am deeply grateful to my parents.

blocks.text: Rule 260
Prepositions like – at, on and in have dual roles, telling both time and place.

items.text: The class is at 8 o'clock. (time)
Meet me at the school. (place)
The election is on Thursday. (time)
Is your name on the ballot? (place)
Spring officially begins in three days. (time)
We're still up to our knees in snow. (place)

blocks.text: Rule 261
Prepositions of direction, like – to, on, onto, in, and into tell you where to go or where to put something.

items.text: It's time to go to the class.
Put on your gloves and shoes.
Make sure your books are in your shelf.

blocks.text: Rule 262

Prepositions 'during' and 'while' are used for referring to something in action. 'During' is a preposition which is used before a noun (during + noun) for saying when something happens. It does not tell us how long it happened.

items.text: Nobody spoke during the presentation.
We get plenty of snow here during winter.
The phone rang while I was watching TV.
I met him while we were studying in the library.

blocks.text: 'While' is used for talking about two things that are happening at the same time. The length of time is not important. Remember : 'while' is used with a subject and a verb (while + subject + verb).
Rule 263
Prepositions – 'onto' and 'into' are used with verbs that imply some sort of movement or progress.

items.text: The plane landed onto the runway. — 'To land' is not a verb which necessarily requires movement; it's referring to the moment when the plane actually stops on the runway. We can say – The plane landed on the runway.
But – The plane glided onto the runway. — 'Gliding' most certainly implies motion, so we can use onto with it.
The caterpillar changed into a butterfly.
The caterpillar changed in a butterfly.
Put the book in the box.
Put the book into the box.

blocks.text: Remember that – 'into' can usually be replaced by in.
Rule 264
Nouns and prepositions often work together in common phrases, like – on vacation, by chance, on purpose, by accident, difference between, on strike, a solution to.

items.text: Can we find a solution to this problem?
There is currently a great demand for organic products.
It's the season for celebration.
What's the cause of this accident?

blocks.text: Rule 265
Adjectives and prepositions are commonly used in phrases. The adjective usually goes before the preposition.

items.text: I'm really excited about this project.
He was found guilty of fraud and tax evasion.
Students often get worried about writing exams.
The world felt sorry for the victims of the tsunami.

blocks.text: Rule 266
Verbs and prepositions are also used in common phrases. The verb generally goes in front of the preposition.

items.text: Do you agree to the new guidelines?
You get what you pay for.
This novel gave me a lot to think about.

blocks.text: Rule 267
The verb and the preposition may be separated, especially if the sentence is formally written so the preposition isn't at the end.

items.text: Didn't I warn you about leaving things until the last minute?
To whom does this book belong? (Who does this book belong to?)
Could you please explain this maths problem to me?

blocks.text: Some other examples of verb/preposition combinations are ask for, depend on, look after, wait for, rely on, dream on, lead on, do something for someone, be careful of, be careful with, be disappointed by, boast about, complain about, in conclusion, and search for.
Rule 268

It's a common rule which states that you should never end a sentence with a preposition. In conversation and informal writing, ending a sentence with a preposition is perfectly acceptable. It's only in formal writing that we still follow the rule.

items.text: Which box should this go into? (Into which box should this go?)
Come in. (Come into the house.)
When I glanced at the table, I saw the dog was hiding beneath. (When I glanced at the table, I saw the dog was hiding beneath it.)

blocks.text: Rule 269
Objective case (of noun or pronoun) is used after a preposition.

items.text: I do not depend on him. — It is wrong to say – I do not depend on he.

blocks.text: Rule 270
A preposition generally, but not always, goes before its noun or pronoun.

items.text: That is something I cannot agree to.
How many of you can I depend on?
But, if you say – Where did you get this at? Where did he go to? — These sentences are wrong. The correct form of these sentences will be – Where did you get this? Where did he go?

blocks.text: The prepositions 'at' and 'to' at the end of these sentences are meaningless and wrong to use.
Rule 271

'Due to' and 'owing to' are similar in meaning to 'on account of' and 'because of'. They are all prepositions used with noun phrases and are often used interchangeably. They indicate that something happened as a result of something or introduce the reason for something happening. Remember, verb add is followed by preposition 'to'.

items.text: He was kept in after school due to/owing to his bad behaviour. = He was kept in after school on account of/because of his bad behaviour.
Due to/owing to a broken propeller, the new cruise liner returned immediately to the port. = The new cruise liner returned immediately to the port because of/on account of a broken propeller.

blocks.text: Rule 272
The preposition 'like' means 'similar to' or 'similarly to'. It should be followed by an object of the preposition (noun, pronoun, noun phrase), not by a subject and verb.

items.text: You look like your mother. — That is, you look similar to her. (Mother is the object of the preposition 'like'.)
But it will be wrong if you say – You look like your mother does. (Avoid 'like' with noun + verb.)

blocks.text: Rule 273
Instead of 'like', use as, as if, as though, or the way while following comparison with a subject and verb.

items.text: You look the way your mother does.
Do as I ask.
Again, if you say – You look like you're angry. It is wrong. The correct sentence will be – You look as if you're angry. (Or, as though)

blocks.text: Rule 274
Follow 'different' with the preposition 'from'. Things differ from other things; avoid 'different than'.

items.text: You're different from me.
It is wrong to say – You're different than I am.

blocks.text: Rule 275
Use 'into' rather than 'in' to express motion towards something. Use 'in' to tell the location.

items.text: I swam in the pool.
I walked into the house.
I looked into the matter.
But if you say – I dived in the water – is wrong. The correct sentence will be – I dived into the water.
Again, if you say – Throw it in the trash – is wrong. The correct sentence will be – Throw it into the trash.

blocks.text: Rule 276
'On' is used for expressing a surface of something.

items.text: Put an egg on the kitchen table.
The paper is on my desk.

blocks.text: Rule 277
'On' is used for specifying days and dates.

items.text: The garbage truck comes on Wednesdays.
I was born on the 14th day of June in 1988.

blocks.text: Rule 278
'On' is used for indicating a device or machine, such as a phone or computer.

items.text: He is on the phone right now.
She has been on the computer since this morning.
My favourite movie will be on TV tonight.

blocks.text: Rule 279
'On' is used for indicating a part of the body.

items.text: The stick hit me on my shoulder.
He kissed me on my cheek.
I wear a ring on my finger.

blocks.text: Rule 280
'On' is used for indicating the state of something.

items.text: Everything in this store is on sale.
The building is on fire.

blocks.text: Rule 281
'At' is used for showing a rate, speed, etc.

items.text: He was driving at 70 mph.
The noise came at a two-minute interval (= once every two minutes).

blocks.text: Rule 282
'At' is used for pointing out specific time.

items.text: I will meet you at 12 p.m.; The bus will stop here at 5:45 p.m.

blocks.text: Rule 283
'At' is used for indicating a place.

items.text: There is a party at the club house.
There were hundreds of people at the park.
We saw a baseball game at the stadium.

blocks.text: Rule 284
'At' is used for indicating an email address.

items.text: Please email me at abc@gmail.com.

blocks.text: Rule 285
'At' is used for  indicating an activity or a cause.

items.text: He laughed at my acting.
I am good at drawing a portrait.

blocks.text: Rule 286
'In' is used for unspecific times during a day, month, season and year.

items.text: She always reads newspapers in the morning.
In summer, we have a rainy season for three weeks.
The new semester will start in March.

blocks.text: Rule 287
'In' is used for indicating a location or place.

items.text: She looked me directly in the eyes.
I am currently staying in a hotel.
My hometown is Los Angeles, which is in California.

blocks.text: Rule 288
'In' is used for indicating a shape, colour or size.

items.text: This painting is mostly in blue.
The students stood in a circle.
This jacket comes in four different sizes.

blocks.text: Rule 289
'In' is used for expressing while doing something.

items.text: In preparing for the final report, we revised the text three times.
A catch phrase needs to be impressive in marketing a product.

blocks.text: Rule 290
'In' is used for indicating a belief, an opinion, an interest or a feeling.

items.text: I believe in the next life; We are not interested in gambling.

blocks.text: Rule 291

The prepositions 'since' and 'for' are used for denoting time. 'Since' is used to mean – from a certain point of time (past till now); while 'for' is used to mean – over a certain period of time (past till now).

items.text: Rahul has been living in Canada since 1980.
Ajay has been working with a publishing house for two years.

blocks.text: Rule 292

Both 'ago' and 'before' are also used for referring to time. 'Ago' is used to mean a certain time in the past; while 'before' is used to mean – earlier than a certain point of time. 'before' also means — in front of

items.text: My uncle visited us two years ago.
Mary came to stay with us before 2005.

blocks.text: Rule 293
Prepositions 'to' and 'past' are used for telling the time.

items.text: The time by the clock is ten to six. (i.e. the time is 5:50)
The train will leave at fifteen past six. (i.e. 6:15)

blocks.text: Rule 294
'To', 'till' and 'until' are used for marking the beginning and end of a period of time.

items.text: Raju goes to office from Monday to Friday.
The office remains open from Monday till Friday.
The principal remains present in the school from morning until the school closes.

blocks.text: Rule 295
You should remember that 'till' and 'until' are also used in the sense of how long something is going to last.

items.text: He is on holiday till / until Friday.

blocks.text: Rule 296
The preposition 'by' is used in the sense of – at the latest.

items.text: I will be back by 6 o' clock.
By 4 pm, I had read five pages of the book.

blocks.text: 'By' is also used for referring to up to a certain time.
Rule 297
The use of 'angry with' and 'angry at' is different. If directed at a person 'angry with' should always be used, while if directed at a situation 'angry at' is used.

items.text: I was very angry with her; I was very angry at how rainy it was.

blocks.text: Rule 298
'By', 'next to'; 'near' and 'beside' are prepositions of place and are used for referring to position or direction, like – left or right of somebody or something.

items.text: Raja is standing by / next to / beside his father's car.
Come and sit beside me.
Your hat is beside the basket.

blocks.text: Rule 299
There is often confusion between the usage of 'under' and 'below'. 'Under' is used for referring to the position – on the ground, lower than (or covered by) something else.

items.text: The bag is under the table.
The fish are below the surface.

blocks.text: 'Below' is used to mean – lower than something else but above ground.
Rule 300
The preposition 'over' has also certain uses. 'Over' is used for referring to something that is covered by something else.

items.text: Put a jacket over your shirt.
You are allowed to enter this cafe if you are over sixteen years of age.
To cross the lake, walk over the bridge.
Climb over the wall.

blocks.text: 'Over' is used to mean 'more than'. 'Over' is used to mean – getting to the other side. 'Over' is also used for referring 'overcoming an obstacle'.
Rule 301
There is also confusion about the usage of 'above' and 'across'. 'Above' is used to mean – higher than something else, but not directly over it.

items.text: There is a path above the lake.
Walk across the bridge to reach the garden.
Swim across the lake to reach the other shore.

blocks.text: 'Across' is used to mean – getting to the other side.
Rule 302
'Through' is a preposition of place and is used for referring to something with limits on top, bottom and the sides.

items.text: The Delhi Metro runs through the tunnel.

blocks.text: Rule 303
'towards', preposition of place, is used to mean – movement in the direction of something (but not directly to it).

items.text: Go five steps towards the house and then take a turn.

blocks.text: Rule 304
Besides other usage, 'at' is also used for age.

items.text: She learnt French at 50.

blocks.text: Rule 305
'Off' is used to mean – leaving a public transport vehicle.

items.text: When you reach the station, get off the train.

blocks.text: Rule 306
The proposition 'out of' is also used to mean – leaving a car or taxi.

items.text: Get out of the taxi.

blocks.text: Rule 307
'Of' is used to mean – who/what does it belong to.

items.text: He showed me a page of the book.
The clip shows the picture of a palace.

blocks.text: 'Of' is also used for referring – what it shows.
Rule 308
The preposition 'by' also refers to 'who made it'.

items.text: Macbeth is a novel by Shakespeare.

blocks.text: Rule 309
'About' is used to mean— on the subject of someone/something; in connection with someone/something.

items.text: We were talking about you.

blocks.text: Rule 310
'On' is used for referring to 'walking or riding on horseback'.

items.text: I go the park in the morning on foot.

blocks.text: Rule 311
'By' has several uses. Besides other usage, 'by' is used to refer to rise or fall of something.

items.text: The price of onion has risen by 30%.
I go to office by bus.

blocks.text: 'By' is also used to mean travelling (other than walking).
Rule 312
The prepositions used after two words must be made clear if these two words are connected by 'and' or 'or'.

items.text: She is conscious of and engaged in her work.
It is wrong to say – She is conscious and engaged in her work.

blocks.text: Rule 313
If a principal verb is used after about, after, at, before, for, from, in, on, to, that verb must be in '-ing' (V4) form.

items.text: You prevented me from doing it.
It is wrong to say – You prevented me from do it.

blocks.text: Rule 314
Remember that – on, in, at are not used before today, tomorrow, yesterday, the following day, the next day, etc.

items.text: He will go there tomorrow.
It is wrong to say – He will go there on tomorrow.

blocks.text: Rule 315
No preposition is used before the word 'home'. But, 'at home' is a phrase which bears a different meaning.

items.text: Bring a T.V. -set home.
It is wrong to say – Bring a T.V. set at home.
My father is not at home.
It is wrong to say– My father is not home.

blocks.text: Rule 316
After transitive verbs, like discuss, describe, reach, order, tell, demand, attack, resemble, ridicule, etc., we directly use the object and no preposition is used after the verb.

items.text: The poet describes the beauty of Nature in this poem.
It is wrong to say – The poet describes about the beauty of Nature in this poem.

blocks.text: Rule 317
Remember that – say / suggest / propose / speak / reply / explain / talk / listen / write / prefer is followed by the preposition 'to' if there is a person in the form of an object.

items.text: He did not reply to me. — It is wrong to say – He did not reply me.
He did not write a letter. — It is wrong to say – He did not write to a letter.

blocks.text: Rule 318
The preposition 'besides' means 'in addition to' or 'apart from'. As an adverb, it means 'furthermore' or 'and another thing'.

items.text: Besides Mohan, who else caught influenza? — (Here, 'besides' is a preposition.)
Besides, it's not just about determination. — (Here, 'besides' is an adverb.)

blocks.text: Rule 319

The word 'among' is usually used for portraying the idea of being part of a group or in the midst of a group. 'Among' is usually followed by a plural noun. The preposition 'among' means – in the company of, by the joint action of, or each with the other. The word 'between' is usually used for describing something being in the middle of two other things. The preposition 'between' means – by the common action of, in point of comparison to, from one to another, or by the combined effort of.

items.text: A discussion is going on among the members of the party.
You are among those who are invited to the function.
There are cultural differences between the Americans and the Canadians.
The award money was divided between Jack and Joe.

blocks.text: In general, between applies to reciprocal arrangements (one member to another member), and among applies to collective arrangements (with all members involved).
Rule 320

'From' can also be used with the prepositions 'to' and 'until' for marking the beginning and ending point of time of an action or state. Generally, 'from ... to' is used with past tense, while 'from ... until' is used while speaking about future actions. However, 'from ... to' can be used in most situations.

items.text: I played tennis from two until four in the afternoon yesterday.
We are meeting in Bangalore from Monday until Thursday.

blocks.text: Rule 321

The prepositions 'in' and 'into' and 'on' and 'onto' have somewhat similar behaviour. 'Into' and 'onto' are used with verbs that show movement. They show both the direction and the result of the movement.

items.text: Ajay dived into the lake.
Harry threw his keys onto the table.
Nadia put the cake in the oven.
The cat jumped onto the sofa.

blocks.text: Rule 322
Conjunctions connect thoughts, ideas, actions, nouns, clauses, etc.

items.text: Mother went to the market and bought fresh vegetables. — In this sentence, the conjunction and connects the two things mother did.
Mother went to the market, and I went to tuition. — Here, and connects two sentences.

blocks.text: Rule 323
You can also use conjunctions to make lists.

items.text: I can't decide between the blue shirt and the red shirt.
We bought burgers, hotdogs and sausages.

blocks.text: Rule 324
While using a conjunction, make sure that the parts which are being joined by the conjunction have a parallel structure (i.e. they use the same verb forms, etc.)

items.text: I worked quickly yet careful. — Here, careful is not in the same form as quickly; this creates faulty parallelism. The parts joined by a conjunction need to be in the same form.
The correct sentence will be – I worked quickly yet carefully. — The two adverbs modify the verb worked.

blocks.text: Rule 325
The coordinating conjunctions are conjunctions that join two independent clauses, or two nouns, or two verbs, etc.

items.text: We didn't have much money, but we were happy. — Here are two contrasting states of being: not having much money, and being happy.

blocks.text: Coordinating conjunctions are – for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so. (You can remember the coordinating conjunctions with the acronym FANBOYS.) Remember that the coordinating conjunction connects the two verbs.
Rule 326
Coordinating conjunctions go in between items joined, not at the beginning or end.

items.text: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.
It is wrong to say – But I don't like tea, I like coffee.

blocks.text: Rule 327
'But' is used both as a conjunction and a preposition. As a conjunction 'but' is used for joining contrasting ideas.

items.text: Their front door was open, but nobody was at home.
The rope was thin but it was strong.
He is hardworking, but not clever.
They are all wrong but me. (= except me.)
All but you loved me for money. (= All except you loved me for money.)
Everybody came but John. (= Everybody came except John.)
We should have enjoyed the journey but for the rain.
He would have helped us but for having no money himself. (—except that he had no money.)
Nobody but him would do a thing like that. (More formal: Nobody but he —)

blocks.text:
'But' as a preposition can mean except after all, none, every, any, no etc.
The expression 'but for' is used for expressing the idea of 'if something had not existed/happened'.
After but we usually use object pronouns. Subject pronouns are also possible in a formal style.
Rule 328
When a coordinating conjunction joins two words, phrases, or subordinate clauses, no comma should be placed before the conjunction.

items.text: Words: bread and butter
Phrases: at the beach or by the lakeside
Subordinate clauses: what you say and what you do

blocks.text: Rule 329
A coordinating conjunction joining three or more words, phrases or subordinate clauses creates a series and requires commas between the elements.

items.text: Words: peanuts, cookies and milk
Phrases: in the mountains, at the beach or by the lakeside
Subordinate clauses: what you think, what you say and what you do

blocks.text: Rule 330
A coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses creates a compound sentence and requires a comma before the coordinating conjunction.

items.text: Raja ate all the peanuts, so Sunil ate the cookies.
I don't care for the beach, but I enjoy a good vacation in the mountains.

blocks.text: Rule 331

Correlative conjunctions are pairs of conjunctions that work together. Some examples of correlative conjunctions are either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also, both/and, although/yet, whether/or, so/that.

items.text: She not only wrote the text but also selected the illustrations.
I have finished both my English essay and my history essay.
You could use either the spoon or the fork.
He would neither eat nor allow us to eat.
It is wrong to say – Neither he would eat nor allow us to eat.
I shall neither follow your instructions nor resign.
It is wrong to say – Neither I shall follow your instructions nor resign.
He visited not only France but also Germany.
It is wrong to say – He not only visited France but also Germany.

blocks.text: Rule 332
'As many as' must be followed by a cardinal number with a plural countable noun (or with a plural countable noun understood).

items.text: He drinks as many as three bottles of milk a day.
The pizza company delivers as many as two hundred pizzas per night.
If you travel by car, it can take as much as 50 litres of petrol to get across Texas.
Katrina could spend as much as ₹ 50,000 on one shopping trip.
He drinks as much as one litre of milk a day.

blocks.text: 'As much as', however, can be followed by a cardinal number with an uncountable noun when it refers to a quantity involving time, money, distance, weight.
Rule 333

The construction 'not only... but also' is called a correlative conjunction. It is used for presenting two related pieces of information. Just remember to use two verbs, two adjectives or two nouns that make chronological sense.

items.text: He's not only funny but also intelligent.
He's not only fat but also tall.
He has not only a sense of humour but also intelligence.

blocks.text:
Remember that when you use a correlative conjunction, both clauses have to be parallel.
Because the subject is after 'not only', there also needs to be a subject after 'but also'.
Rule 334

Subordinating conjunctions show a relationship between an independent and a dependent clause; some of the relationships can be cause-and-effect, and contrast. Some of the subordinating conjunctions are because, since, as, although, though, while and whereas.

items.text: I can stay out until the clock strikes twelve. — Here, the subordinating conjunction is connecting the two ideas: I can stay out and the clock strikes twelve.

blocks.text: Rule 335

The subordinating conjunction doesn't need to go in the middle of the sentence. It must be part of the dependent clause, but it doesn't matter whether the clause is the first or second one in the sentence.

items.text: Before he leaves, make sure his room is clean.

blocks.text: Rule 336
If the dependent clause comes first, you'll need to use a comma; but if the independent clause comes first, you probably won't need a comma.

items.text: Because I was thirsty, I drank a glass of water.
I drank a glass of water because I was thirsty.

blocks.text: Rule 337
Two conjunctions should not be used in the same sentence.

items.text: Although she was tired yet she went on working.
It is wrong to say – Although she was tired yet she still went on working.

blocks.text: Rule 338

Conjunctive adverbs are adverbs which join two clauses. Some examples of conjunctive adverbs are also, besides, accordingly, finally, subsequently, therefore, thus, meanwhile, moreover, nonetheless, instead, however, indeed, hence, consequently, similarly and still.

items.text: Please close the outer door; otherwise, the cold air comes in.
First feed the poor; next, please feed the guests.

blocks.text: Conjunctive adverbs frequently (but not necessarily) have a semi-colon before them. As they're conjunctions (i.e. words that join two thoughts or ideas), it's best not to use them at the beginning of a sentence.
Rule 339
Conjunctive adverbs can also put a little break in the sentence, providing emphasis.

items.text: The new building will, furthermore, provide storage facilities as well as meeting space.

blocks.text: However, if the interruption in the sentence should be weaker, you can leave out the commas, like – The new building will furthermore provide storage facilities as well as meeting space.
Rule 340
The preposition 'for' (is used to mean seeing that, since or because) and 'yet' (is used to mean though, still, or nevertheless) can only join clauses.

items.text: John thought he had a good chance to get the job, for his father was on the company's board of trustees.
John plays basketball well, yet his favourite sport is badminton.

blocks.text:
The word 'for' is most often used as a preposition, but it does serve, on rare occasions, as a coordinating conjunction. 'For' has serious sequential implications and in its use the order of thoughts is more important than it is, say, with because or since. Its function is to introduce the reason for the preceding clause.
The word 'yet' functions sometimes as an adverb and has several meanings: in addition, even, still, eventually, and so soon as now. It also functions as a coordinating conjunction meaning something like 'nevertheless' or 'but'.
Rule 341
Adversative conjunctions, like – but, still, yet, whereas, while, nevertheless, etc. express contrast between two statements.

items.text: The rope was thin but it was strong.
She is poor but she is happy.
He is hardworking whereas his brother is quite the reverse.

blocks.text: Rule 342
Conjunctions which present two alternatives are called disjunctive or alternative conjunctions. (or, either...or, neither...nor, otherwise, else, etc. are disjunctive conjunctions)

items.text: She must weep, or she will die.
Either he is mad or he feigns madness.

blocks.text: Rule 343
Some coordinating conjunctions express something inferred from another statement or fact. These are called illative conjunctions. (for and so are illative conjunctions)

items.text: Somebody came, for I heard a knock at the door.
He must be asleep, for there is no light in his room.
He has been working hard, so he will pass.

blocks.text: Rule 344
The preposition 'and' joins two propositions (ideas).

items.text: (1) One idea is chronologically sequential to another. — Rashmi sent in her application and waited by the phone for a response.
(2) One idea is the result of another. — Rajiv heard the weather report and promptly boarded up his house.
(3) One idea is in contrast to another. — Parul is brilliant and Jasmine has a pleasant personality.
(4) An element of surprise. — Dubai is a rich city and suffers from many symptoms of urban blight.
(5) One clause is dependent upon another, conditionally. (Usually the first clause is an imperative) — Use your credit cards frequently and you'll soon find yourself deep in debt.
(6) A kind of comment on the first clause. — Suraj became addicted to gambling — and that surprised no one who knew him.

blocks.text: Rule 345
The coordinating conjunction 'nor' is used in negative expressions.

items.text: He is neither sane nor brilliant.
That is neither what I said nor what I meant.

blocks.text: Rule 346
'But' is a coordinating conjunction that joins two contrasting propositions (ideas).

items.text: A contrast that is unexpected in light of the first clause. — Javed lost a fortune in the stock market, but he still seems able to live quite comfortably.
An affirmative sense what the first part of the sentence implied in a negative way — The company never invested foolishly, but used the services of a sage investment counsellor.
To connect two ideas with the meaning of 'with the exception of' (and then the second word takes over as the subject) — Everybody but Ramesh is trying out for the team.

blocks.text: Rule 347
The coordinating conjunction 'or' joins two alternative propositions (ideas) –

items.text: To suggest that only one possibility can be realized, excluding one or the other — You can study hard for this exam or you can fail.
To suggest the inclusive combination of alternatives — We can broil chicken on the grill tonight, or we can just eat leftovers.
To suggest a refinement of the first clause — Presidency College is the premier college in the country, or so it seems to most Presidency College alumnae.
To suggest a restatement or 'correction' of the first part of the sentence — There are no rattlesnakes in this canyon, or so our guide tells us.
To suggest a negative condition — The New Hampshire state motto is rather grim 'Live free or die.'
To suggest a negative alternative without the use of an imperative — They must approve his political style or they wouldn't keep electing him mayor.

blocks.text: Rule 348
The conjunction 'as' is often confused with 'like'. It is followed by a clause. Like is a preposition. It is followed by a noun or a noun equivalent.

items.text: He fought like a lion.
It is wrong to say – He fought as a lion.
He fought as a lion does.
It is wrong to say – He fought like a lion does.

blocks.text: Rule 349
'As' can be used in the sense of 'though'.

items.text: Though he was sick yet he worked diligently.
Sick as he was, he worked diligently.
Though he was young yet he fought valiantly.
Young as he was, he fought valiantly.

blocks.text: Rule 350
The conjunctions 'as if' and 'as though' are used more or less synonymously. Both of them show condition.

items.text: She spoke as if she knew everything. (She spoke as though she knew everything.)
It looks as if/ as though it might rain.
The floods were rising and it was as if it were the end of the world.
It looks as if they had a shock.
It looks as though you had not met before.
It doesn't look as if the economy would improve any time soon.
You look as if you had seen a ghost.

blocks.text: Rule 351
'Until' and 'Unless' are conjunctions which can be used together in a complimentary way as a sort of set phrase, but the meanings of these two conjunctions are different.

items.text: You are unlikely to earn decent money until you start working hard.
I won't start the project till I hear that all the plans have been approved.
She resigned in March but continued to draw her salary till the end of May.
Please wait in the waiting room until they call your name.
I shall not refund you your money unless you send me the original receipt.
I can't help you unless you tell me what's wrong.
Unless you obey my instructions, you will be dismissed. Or, if you don't obey my instructions, you will be dismissed.
But it is wrong to say— unless you don't obey my instructions, you will be dismissed.

blocks.text:
'Until / Till' means – up to a particular point in time.
'Until' and 'Till' can be used both as conjunctions and prepositions and that 'till' is the informal equivalent of 'until'.
Unless' means – if not this, then that.
We use unless to indicate that something else will happen as a result of this if something does not happen.
Unless means 'if not, and hence there is no need to add another 'not' in the following clause.
Rule 352
Not/Never is followed by 'or'

items.text: He warned we not to be late or forget to come.
Never fear or lose courage.

blocks.text: Rule 353
Seldom if never/seldom or never is the correct expression.

items.text: She seldom if ever, goes to the theatre.
The national network seldom or never telecasts good programmes.

blocks.text: Note : The use of seldom or ever in place of seldom or never is inappropriate.
Rule 354
'So as' indicates purpose.

items.text: We started early so as to get a good seat.

blocks.text: Rule 355
' Such as' indicates result.

items.text: His actions were such as to offend everyone.

blocks.text: Rule 356
'Than' is a subordinating conjunction. It is usually followed by an object pronoun or a subject pronoun + verb.

items.text: She is taller than him.
She is taller than he is.
She earns more than him.
She earns more than he does.

blocks.text: Rule 357

'Lest' means 'that...not' and hence it is wrong to add another 'not' in the following clause. Another point that needs to be noted is that the only auxiliary that can be used after 'lest' is 'should'.

items.text: Take care lest you should fall.
But it is wrong to say – Take care lest you do not fall/fall.

blocks.text: Rule 358
'That' should not be used before the question words – what, when, where, whether and why.

items.text: He asked me what my name was.
But it is wrong to say – He asked me that what was my name.

blocks.text: Rule 359

The expression 'no sooner...than' is used for suggesting that one action or situation takes place/took place immediately after another action or situation. When 'no sooner' goes at the beginning of the sentence, we use an inverted word order. That means the auxiliary verb goes before the subject.

items.text: (1) The train arrived at the station. Soon the passengers rushed towards it. — No sooner had the train arrived at the station than the passengers rushed towards it.
(2) The teacher entered the classroom. Suddenly the students stood up. — No sooner did the teacher enter the classroom than the students stood up.

blocks.text: Rule 360
It is wrong to use 'when' instead of 'than' in no sooner – than construction.

items.text: No sooner did the lion appear than he shot it down.
It is wrong to say – No sooner did the lion appear when he shot it down.

blocks.text: Rule 361
If a sentence begins with 'no sooner', it should be immediately followed by 'had' or 'did'.

items.text: No sooner did the lion appear than he shot it down.
It is wrong to say – No sooner the lion appeared than he shot it down.

blocks.text: Rule 362

The coordinating conjunction 'so' used for referring to the first idea (the cause) results in the second idea (the effect). Remember that sometimes 'so' can connect two independent clauses along with a comma, but sometimes it can't. 'So' means 'as well' or 'in addition'.

items.text: Arnold is not the only athlete in his family, so are his brother, sister, and his Uncle Rajat.
Lucky has always been nervous in large gatherings, so it is no surprise that he avoids crowds of his adoring fans.

blocks.text: Rule 363
'Hardly' and 'scarcely' should be followed by 'when' or 'before', but not by 'than' or 'that'.

items.text: Hardly did I reach the station when the train left it.
It is wrong to say – Hardly did I reach the station, than the train left it.

blocks.text: Rule 364
You can express an idea using hardly/scarcely…when in the form of correlative.

items.text: Hardly had I reached the station when the train came.
Scarcely had I reached the station when the train arrived.

blocks.text: Rule 365
'That' should not be used before a sentence in Direct Speech and before Interrogative adverbs and pronouns in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: He said, "I shall go there." — It is wrong to say – He said that, "I shall go there."
He asked me who I was. — It is wrong to say – He asked me that who I was.

blocks.text: Rule 366
If 'scarcely' begins the sentence, it should be immediately followed by 'had'.

items.text: Scarcely had I reached the station when the train steamed out.
I had scarcely reached the station when the train steamed out.
But it is wrong to say – Scarcely I had reached the station when the train steamed out.

blocks.text: Rule 367
'None other than' is a phrase which is used when you want to show that someone or something is a surprising or exciting choice or example.

items.text: The first Independence speech was given by none other than Pt. Nehru.

blocks.text: Look at the sentence : Her first customer was none other than Mrs. Tendulkar.
Rule 368
A gerund is formed by adding –ing to a verb. It functions as a noun.

items.text: Swimming is very good for the body.
Smoking is prohibited in the hospital. — Here, 'swimming' and 'smoking' are gerunds.

blocks.text: Rule 369
A gerund can also be used as a direct object.

items.text: They do not appreciate my singing. — Here, 'singing' is a gerund.

blocks.text: Rule 370
A gerund can also be used as a subject complement.

items.text: My cat's favourite activity is sleeping. — Here, the gerund is 'sleeping'.

blocks.text: Rule 371
You can also use a gerund as an object of a preposition.

items.text: The police arrested him for speeding. — Here, the gerund is 'speeding'.

blocks.text: Rule 372
The gerund phrase functions as the subject of the sentence.

items.text: Finding a needle in a haystack would be easier than what we're trying to do. — Here, 'Finding' is gerund; 'a needle' is the direct object of action expressed in gerund; and 'in a haystack' is the prepositional phrase.
Being the boss made Raghav feel uneasy. — Here, 'being' is gerund; 'the boss' is the subject complement for Raghav via state of being expressed in gerund.

blocks.text: Rule 373
The gerund phrase functions as the direct object of the verb.

items.text: I hope that you appreciate my offering you this opportunity. — Here, 'my' is a possessive pronoun (adjective form), modifying the gerund; 'offering' is gerund; 'you' is indirect object of action expressed in gerund; and 'this opportunity' is the direct object of action expressed in gerund.

blocks.text: Rule 374
The gerund phrase functions as the subject complement.

items.text: Ajit's favourite tactic has been jabbering away to his constituents. — Here, 'jabbering away to' is gerund phrase; and 'his constituents' is the direct object of action expressed in gerund.

blocks.text: Rule 375
The gerund phrase functions as the object of the preposition 'for'.

items.text: You might get in trouble for faking an illness to avoid work. — Here, 'faking' is gerund; 'an illness' is the direct object of action expressed in gerund; and 'to avoid work' is the infinitive phrase.

blocks.text: Rule 376
An infinitive is formed by using the word 'to' before the verb in its stem word. It functions as a noun, an adjective or adverb.

items.text: He was made to clean his room.
Anuj loves to talk.

blocks.text: Rule 377
An adverb or adverbial phrase should not be placed between 'to' and verbal part of the infinitive. (This is called the split infinitive.)

items.text: I hoped to reply immediately to your letter.
It is wrong to say – I hoped to immediately reply to your letter.

blocks.text: Rule 378
An infinitive should be in the present tense unless it represents an action prior to that of the governing verb.

items.text: I should have liked to go there.
It is wrong to say – I should have liked to have gone there.

blocks.text: Rule 379
Gerunds are the 'ing' forms of the verbs (verb + ing). Gerunds are used after certain verbs.

items.text: I enjoy singing.

blocks.text: Rule 380
Gerunds are also used after prepositions.

items.text: I drank a cup of coffee before leaving.

blocks.text: Rule 381
Gerunds are used as the subject or object of a sentence.

items.text: Swimming is a good exercise.

blocks.text: Rule 382
We use 'to' + infinitive after certain verbs.

items.text: We decided to leave.

blocks.text: Rule 383
We use 'to' + infinitive after many adjectives.

items.text: It's difficult to get up early.

blocks.text: Rule 384
We use 'to' + infinitive to show purpose.

items.text: I came to London to study English.

blocks.text: Rule 385
We use the bare-infinitive (the infinitive without 'to') after modal verbs.

items.text: I can meet you at six o'clock.

blocks.text: Rule 386
We use the bare-infinitive after 'let', 'make' and (sometimes) 'help'.

items.text: The teacher let us leave early.
Make the child sweep. Help him (to) do his work.

blocks.text: Rule 387
We use the bare-infinitive after some verbs of perception (see, watch, hear, notice, feel, sense)

items.text: I watched her walk away.

blocks.text: Rule 388
We use the bare-infinitive after expressions with 'why'.

items.text: Why go out at night before an exam ?
Why join any institute ?

blocks.text: Rule 389
We use 'used to + infinitive' to talk about habits or repeated actions in the past which we don't do in the present. We also use it to talk about states in the past which are no longer true.

items.text: I used to have long hair (but now I have short hair).
He used to smoke (but now he doesn't smoke).

blocks.text: Rule 390
We can also use 'would + infinitive' to talk about a habit or repeated action in the past. We usually use 'would + infinitive' in this way when we're telling a story about the past.

items.text: When I was a student, we would often have a drink after the class on Friday.
When I lived in Italy, we would go to a little restaurant near our house.

blocks.text: Rule 391
But we don't use 'would + infinitive' to talk about states in the past. So, if we're talking about the past, we can't say:

items.text: I would have long hair.
I would live in Canada.

blocks.text: Rule 392
The to-infinitive is used for indicating the purpose or intention of an action. In this case, 'to' has the same meaning as 'in order to' or 'so as to'.

items.text: He came to collect his pay cheque.
The three bears went to find firewood.
I am calling to ask you about dad.
Your sister has gone to finish her homework.

blocks.text: Rule 393
The to-infinitive is also used as the subject of the sentence.

items.text: To be or not to be, that is the question.
To know her is to love her.
To visit the Giza Pyramid is my life-long dream.
To understand statistics, that is our aim.

blocks.text: Rule 394
The to-infinitive is used for indicating what something can or will be used for. In this pattern, the to-infinitive follows a noun or pronoun.

items.text: The children need a garden to play in.
I would like a sandwich to eat.
I don't have anything to wear.
Would you like something to drink?

blocks.text: Rule 395

The to-infinitive can also be used after adjectives. There is a common pattern using the to-infinitive with an adjective. These phrases are formed: subject + to be + adjective + (for / of someone) + to-infinitive + (rest of sentence)

items.text: It is good of you to talk to me.
It is important for Raju to be patient with his little brother.

blocks.text: Rule 396
The to-infinitive is used for making a comment or judgement. To use the to-infinitive while making a comment or judgement about a noun, the pattern is: Subject + to be + noun phrase + to-infinitive

items.text: That is a dangerous way to drive.
What you said was a rude thing to say.

blocks.text: Rule 397

The to-infinitive is used frequently with the adverbs 'too' and 'enough' to express the reasoning behind our satisfaction or dissatisfaction. The pattern is that 'too' and 'enough' are placed before or after the adjective, adverb, or noun that they modify in the same way they would be without the to-infinitive.

items.text: There's too much sugar to put in this bowl.
I had too many books to carry.
This soup is too hot to eat.

blocks.text: Rule 398

The to-infinitive is used with question words. Each of the verbs ask, decide, explain, forget, know, show, tell and understand can be followed by a question word, such as where, how, what, who and when + the to-infinitive.

items.text: She asked me how to use the washing machine.
Do you understand what to do?
Tell me when to press the button.

blocks.text: Rule 399
The zero infinitive is not used after auxiliaries.

items.text: She can't speak to you.
He should give her some money.
Shall I talk to him?

blocks.text: Rule 400
The zero infinitive is used after the verbs of perception. With verbs of perception, the pattern is : verb + object + zero infinitive.

items.text: He saw her fall from the cliff.
We heard them close the door.
They saw us walk towards the lake.

blocks.text: Rule 401
The zero infinitive is used after the verbs 'make' and 'let'.

items.text: Her parents let her stay out late.
Let's go to the cinema tonight.
You made me come with you.

blocks.text: Rule 402
The zero infinitive is used after the expression 'had better'.

items.text: We had better take some warm clothing.
You'd better give me your address.
They had better work harder on their homework.

blocks.text: Rule 403
The zero infinitive is used with 'why'. The question word why is followed by the zero infinitive while making suggestions.

items.text: Why wait until tomorrow?
Why not ask him now?
Why not buy a new car?

blocks.text: Rule 404
The word 'go' + 'sports or recreational activities' usually takes a gerund.

items.text: Let's go shopping; They went skiing.

blocks.text: Rule 405
After a preposition you should use a gerund.

items.text: I will talk with you before going to lunch.
I am looking forward to working with you.

blocks.text: Rule 406
Remember that expressions with the words 'have', 'spend' and 'waste' take a gerund.

items.text: She had fun skiing; He wasted all his time worrying.

blocks.text: Rule 407

The gerund is commonly used after quite a few different verbs, which can be followed by nouns instead of gerunds. Remember, gerunds always function as nouns in sentences. Some of these verbs can also be followed by a that-clause.

items.text: I avoid going to the dentist.
I miss taking walks in the morning.
I have finished working.

blocks.text: A few verbs which can be followed by nouns or gerunds are: avoid, celebrate, consider, contemplate, defer, delay, detest, dislike, dread, enjoy, entail, escape, excuse, finish, forgive, involve, keep, loathe, mind, miss, pardon, postpone, prevent, resent, resist, risk, save, stop, etc.
Rule 408
In many cases, the infinitive form is used for showing the 'intention or purpose'.

items.text: We are here to help; He left to catch the train.

blocks.text: Rule 409
The infinitive form is also used for showing the reason.

items.text: We were sad to hear about your difficulties.
She was shocked to learn the truth.

blocks.text: Rule 410
Infinitives and infinitive phrases can be both subjects and objects in sentences.

items.text: To study hard will increase your chances of getting into college. (Subject)
Kathy wants to study with her friends. (Object)

blocks.text: Rule 411
There are some verbs, like hesitate, offer, promise and want, that are followed only by infinitives.

items.text: She didn't hesitate to tell the boss that some employees were stealing office supplies.
The Kapoor Family offered to watch their neighbour's dog for the whole week.
The school promised to help me find an apartment.
We want to visit all of the historic sites in Egypt.

blocks.text: Rule 412
Infinitives are more often used for answering 'why'-questions.

items.text: Prem: I stopped.
Raja: Why?
Prem: I stopped to take rest.
I stopped in order to take rest.
It is wrong to say – I stopped in order to taking rest.

blocks.text: Again, the phrase 'in order to' is often used in this situation. Therefore, Prem could have said, "I stopped in order to take rest." 'In order to' is also used for answering 'why'-questions. Remember that 'in order to' is never used with gerund.
Rule 413
Gerunds are usually not used for answering 'why'-questions. Gerunds are verbal nouns. Gerunds directly receive actions just like other nouns.

items.text: I stopped the car.
I stopped the thief.
I stopped the child. — Here, the words 'car', 'thief' and 'child' are all nouns.

blocks.text: Rule 414
Infinitives in the subject position are often used for general or habitual actions.

items.text: To err is human, to forgive, divine.
To live a happy life is everyone's deepest desire.
To fix a car requires a lot more than a screwdriver.

blocks.text: Rule 415
When an action has happened in the past, a gerund is used.

items.text: Past action: Monika has studied German.
Gerund referring to past action: Studying German was easy for her.

blocks.text: Rule 416
Ask, advise, allow, command, force, forbid, invite, encourage, compel, beg, order, imagine, instruct, permit, persuade, tell, require, remind, teach, etc. are followed by 'Object + to + V1'.

items.text: He advised me to do it.
It is wrong to say – He advised to do it by me.
She was permitted to go with him.

blocks.text: But when these are used in Passive Voice, then they are followed by 'to +V1'.
Rule 417
Remember : 'know' is followed by how / where / when / why and infinitive.

items.text: I know how to write a letter.
It is wrong to say – I know to write a letter.

blocks.text: Rule 418
When two infinitive structures are joined by and, or, except, but, than, as or like, the second is often without 'to'.

items.text: It is as easy to smile as frown.
Do you want to have lunch now or wait till later?
We had nothing to do except look at the cinema posters.

blocks.text: Rule 419
After modal auxiliary verbs will, shall, would, should, can, could, may, might and must, we use the infinitive without 'to'.

items.text: I shall write to him. (Not – I shall to write...)
We can manage it. (Not – We can to manage...)
I will say what I like.
We must get someone to paint the roof.
Can you help us?
She helped (to) organize a party.

blocks.text: Rule 420
The infinitive 'without to' is not generally used after 'need'. But in some exceptional cases, infinitive 'without to' can be used after 'need' and 'dare'.

items.text: You need not make such a fuss over it.
How dare you call me a liar?
He wondered whether they need to send a deposit. (Incorrect) ↓ Infinitive with 'to'
He wondered whether they need send a deposit. (Correct) ↓ Infinitive without 'to'

blocks.text: Rule 421
After 'do', we use the infinitive without 'to'.

items.text: Do you think she is ready?; I do admit that I was wrong.

blocks.text: Rule 422
After certain verbs like bid, watch, see, let, make and hear, infinitives are used without 'to'.

items.text: They made me wait. (Not – They made me to wait.)
He bade me come. (Not – He bade me to come.)
I saw her light the lamp. (Not – I saw her to light...)
We heard her sing a song. (Not – We heard her to sing...)
We watched them play.
Let him go.
She helped the child (to) lift the box.
She was heard to sing a song.
He was helped to lift the box.
She was made to pay back the money.

blocks.text: 'Help' can also be used in this way. In passive versions of these structures the infinitive is used 'with to'.
Rule 423
After rather, better and had better, we use the infinitive 'without to'.

items.text: You had better consult a doctor.
I would rather go alone.
He would rather die than yield to pressure.

blocks.text: Rule 424
After let, bid, behold, watch, see, feel, make, etc., we use bare-infinitive and not 'to' infinitive.

items.text: I heard him speak on several subjects.
It is wrong to say – I heard him to speak on several subjects.

blocks.text: Rule 425
Bare-infinitive is used after modal auxiliaries, like can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, dare not, need not.

items.text: You need not work hard.
It is wrong to say – You need not to work hard.

blocks.text: Rule 426
The use of 'may' and 'might' is different. We can use 'may' to ask for permission. Infinitive without 'to' is used after these verbs.

items.text: May I borrow your pen? ; May I go now?
It may rain later today; I may not have time to do it today.
She might be at home by now but it's not sure at all.
It might rain this afternoon.
I might not have time to go to the shops for you.
I might not go.
He might have tried to call while I was out.
I might have dropped it in the street.

blocks.text: We use 'may' to suggest something is possible. We use 'might' to suggest a small possibility of something. Remember that 'might' suggests a smaller possibility than 'may'. There is, in fact, little difference and 'might is more usual than 'may'. To state anything in the past using 'might', we use 'might have'.
Rule 427
Had better, had rather, had as soon...as, had sooner, etc. are followed by bare-infinitive.

items.text: He had better go now.
It is wrong to say – He had better to go now.

blocks.text: Rule 428
Conjunction 'than' is also followed by bare-infinitive.

items.text: He had better read than write.
It is wrong to say – He had better read than to write.

blocks.text: Rule 429
When 'but' is used as a preposition and preceded by any form of the verb 'do', then but is followed by bare-infinitive.

items.text: He did nothing but wander.
It is wrong to say – He did nothing but to wander.

blocks.text: Rule 430
Every participle must have a subject of reference.

items.text: It being a rainy day, Vijay decided to stay at home.
It is wrong to say – Being a rainy day, Vijay decided to stay at home.

blocks.text: Rule 431
For completed action, 'having + V3' is used in Active Voice, whereas 'having + been + V3' or 'being + V3' is used in Passive Voice. After should not be used in such a sentence.

items.text: The leader having been killed, the followers ran away.
It is wrong to say – After the leader having been killed, the followers ran away.

blocks.text: Rule 432
Participles – like considering, judging, referring, concerning, regarding, viewing, broadly speaking, etc. do not take any subject of reference.

items.text: Considering the case, I took the decision. — Here, 'I' is not a subject of reference of considering. So, there is no subject of reference for considering; still the sentence is correct.

blocks.text: Rule 433
A participle is usually formed by adding –ing or –ed to a verb. It functions as an adjective.

items.text: The singing bird was the main attraction at the event.
The injured man was waiting for the doctor.

blocks.text: Rule 434
Past participles do not have a consistent ending. The past participles of all regular verbs end in 'ed'; the past participles of irregular verbs, however, vary considerably.

items.text: bring – brought – brought
sing – sang – sung — Here, their past participles —'brought' and 'sung'— do not follow the same pattern even though both verbs have 'ing' at the end. (We use 'ing' to make Present Participle.)

blocks.text: Rule 435
A participle phrase acts like an adjective.

items.text: The man carrying the bricks is my father. — (The participle phrase carrying the bricks describe the man.)
She showed us a plate of scones crammed with cream. — (The participle phrase crammed with cream describe the scones.)
Whistling the same tune as always, John touched the front of his cap with his forefinger. — (The participle phrase Whistling the same tune as always describes John.)
Stunned by the blow, Arun quickly gathered his senses and searched frantically for the pepper spray. — (The participle phrase Stunned by the blow describes Arun.)

blocks.text: Rule 436
The Present participle is the –ing form. You can see this form – (1) in progressive / continuous tenses (e. g. Present Progressive) (2) as an adjective form (3) as a gerund

items.text: I am speaking.
The film is interesting.
He is afraid of flying.

blocks.text: Remember that Present participles are not just used as adjectives. They are also used for forming verb tenses.
Rule 437

The present participle can also be used after the verbs of the senses if we do not want to emphasise that the action was completed. These verbs are – feel, find, hear, listen to, notice, see, smell, watch, etc.

items.text: Did you see him dancing?

blocks.text: Rule 438
The present participle can be used for shortening or combining active clauses that have the same subject.

items.text: She left the house and whistled. Or, She left the house whistling.

blocks.text: Rule 439
Past participles have various endings, usually -ed, -d, -t, -en or -n.

items.text: A swollen eye is God's way of telling you to improve your interpersonal skills.
Do not waste time staring at a closed door.

blocks.text: Rule 440
You can know the form of the Past participle – (1) from perfect tenses (2) from passive voice (3) as an adjective form

items.text: I have spoken.
The letter was written.
I was bored to death.

blocks.text: Rule 441
The past participle can also be used for shortening or combining passive clauses that have the same subject.

items.text: The boy was given an apple. He stopped crying. Or Given an apple, the boy stopped crying.

blocks.text: Rule 442

The Perfect participle can be used for shortening or combining clauses that have the same subject if – (1) one action (the one where the perfect participle is used) is completed before the next action starts. (2) one action has been going on for a period of time when another action starts.

items.text: She bought a bike and cycled home. Or Having bought a bike, she cycled home.
He had been living there for such a long time that he didn't want to move to another town. Or Having lived there for such a long time, he didn't want to move to another town.

blocks.text: Rule 443
The perfect participle can be used for active and passive voice.

items.text: Active voice: having + past participle (Having cooked, he set the table.)
Passive voice: having been + past participle (Having been cooked, the food looked delicious.)

blocks.text: Rule 444
If a clause is shortened using a participle construction, the clause is called participle clause.

items.text: Watching TV, she forgot everything around her.

blocks.text: Rule 445
The Participle clauses can be used even if the clauses to be combined do not have the same subject.

items.text: I heard him playing the guitar. — Here, the participle clause must directly follow the object it is relating to.

blocks.text: Rule 446
A participle construction can also be made if both the subjects are mentioned (often the word 'with' is put before the subject in the participle clause).

items.text: Mrs Jones went to New York. Mr Smith took up her position. → (With) Mrs Jones going to New York, Mr Smith took up her position.

blocks.text: Rule 447
The participle clause and the main clause should have the same subject.

items.text: I was driving on the motorway, when the baby started to cry.
While I was driving on the motorway, the baby started to cry.

blocks.text: Rule 448
In the present tense, nouns and verbs form plurals in opposite ways: nouns add an 's' to the singular form; verbs remove the 's' or 'es' from the singular form.

items.text: The dog chases the cat. (Singular) — Here 'dog' is a noun and subject which is singular with no 's' and 'chases' is a verb with singular 's'.
The dogs chase the cat. (Plural) — Here, 'dogs' is plural with 's' and 'chase' is also plural with no 's'.

blocks.text: Rule 449
Singular subjects need singular verbs, while plural subjects need plural verbs.

items.text: My brother is an engineer.
My sisters are doctors.
The police are blocking off the street where the accident occurred.

blocks.text: But there is an exception with the word 'police'. 'Police' is plural because it is not used for one person of police but when we use this word, it tells about the whole group of the police so it is plural.
Rule 450
Two singular subjects connected by 'or' or 'nor' require a singular verb.

items.text: My aunt or my uncle is arriving by train today.

blocks.text: Rule 451
Two singular subjects connected by 'either/or' or 'neither/nor' require a singular verb.

items.text: Neither Ramesh nor Paresh is available.
Either Julie or Aruna is helping today with stage decorations.

blocks.text: Rule 452

When the subjects joined by 'either - or' neither - nor' are of different persons, the verb will agree in person and number with the subject nearest to it. Also, the plural subject must be placed nearest to the verb.

items.text: Neither you nor he is to take up this task.
It is wrong to say – Neither you nor he are to take up this task.
Either the Chief Minister or the Cabinet Ministers are responsible for this problem.
It is wrong to say – Either the Chief Minister or the Cabinet Ministers is responsible for this problem.
Either you or I am responsible for this mistake.
It is wrong to say – Either you or I are responsible for this mistake.

blocks.text: Rule 453
The subject-verb agreement rules do not apply to verbs used in the simple past tense without any helping verbs.

items.text: The boy talked to me. (Singular)
The boys talked to me. (Plural)

blocks.text: Rule 454
The verb in an 'or', 'either/or', or 'neither/nor' sentence agrees with the noun or pronoun closest to it.

items.text: Neither the plates nor the serving bowl goes on that shelf.
Neither the serving bowl nor the plates go on that shelf.

blocks.text: Rule 455
We use 'neither' while referring to two items and 'none' while referring to more than two items or to an uncountable noun.

items.text: Neither of the two candidates is very impressive.
None of the four candidates impress us.

blocks.text: Rule 456
Two singular subjects connected by either... or, /or/neither... nor require a singular verb.

items.text: My aunt or my uncle is arriving by train today.
Neither Ravi nor Kiran is available.
Either John or Prem is helping today with stage decorations.

blocks.text: Rule 457

Sometimes the subject is separated from the verb by such words as 'along with', 'as well as', 'besides', 'not', etc. These words and phrases are not part of the subject. You should use a singular verb when the subject is singular.

items.text: The politician, along with the newsmen, is expected shortly.
Excitement, as well as nervousness, is the cause of her shaking.

blocks.text: Rule 458
When as well as is part of the subject, the verb must agree with the noun before as well as.

items.text: John, as well as Mary, want to drop the course. — This sentence is wrong as the verb want must agree with the noun preceding as well as in this case. The correct sentence will be – John, as well as Mary, wants to drop the course.

blocks.text: Rule 459

With words that indicate portions, like 'a lot', 'a majority', 'some', 'all' etc. we are guided by the noun after 'of'. Remember that, if the noun after 'of' is singular, you should use a singular verb, and if it is a plural, use a plural verb.

items.text: A lot of the pie has disappeared.
A lot of the pies have disappeared.
Some of the pie is missing.
Some of the pies are missing.

blocks.text: Rule 460
In sentences beginning with here or there, the true subject follows the verb. The subject will always be placed after the verb, so care needs to be taken to identify it correctly.

items.text: There are four hurdles to jump; There is a high hurdle to jump.
Here are the keys ; There is a problem with the balance sheet.
Here are the papers you requested.

blocks.text: Rule 461
Use a singular verb with distances, periods of time, sums of money, etc., when considered as a unit.

items.text: Three miles is too far to walk.
Five years is the maximum sentence for that offence.

blocks.text: Rule 462

The usage of more than one verb in the same clause or sentence can lead to sentence structure error. However, if there is any such kind of usage, the easiest way to fix double verb error is to add a relative pronoun (such as 'that', 'which' or 'who') so that you may create a new subject for one of the verbs.

items.text: People own cars must pay high costs for insurance. (Incorrect)
People (who own cars) must pay high costs for insurance. (Correct)

blocks.text: Rule 463
Some collective nouns, such as family, couple, staff, audience, etc. may take either a singular or a plural verb, depending on their use in the sentence.

items.text: The staff is in a meeting. — Here, Staff is acting as a unit.
The couple disagree about disciplining their child. — Here, the couple refers to two people who are acting as individuals.

blocks.text: Rule 464
The word 'were' replaces 'was' in a sentence that expresses a wish or is contrary to fact.

items.text: If Joe were here, you'd be sorry. — Here, you might think that 'Joe' should not be followed by 'were' but 'was', as 'Joe' is singular. But 'Joe' isn't actually here, so we say 'were', not 'was'. The sentence demonstrates the subjunctive mood, which is used for expressing things that are hypothetical, wishful, imaginary or factually contradictory. The subjunctive mood pairs singular subjects with what we usually think of as plural verbs.
(1) I wish it were Friday.
(2) She requested that he raise his hand.

blocks.text: In the first example, a wishful statement, not a fact, is being expressed; therefore, were, which we usually think of as a plural verb, is used with the singular subject I. Normally, he raise would sound terrible to us. However, in the second example, where a request is being expressed, the subjunctive mood is correct.
Rule 465
Don't get confused by the words that come between the subject and verb; they do not affect agreement.

items.text: The dog, which is chewing on my jeans, is usually very good.

blocks.text: Rule 466
Prepositional phrases between the subject and verb usually do not affect agreement.

items.text: The colours of the rainbow are beautiful.

blocks.text: Rule 467
Subjects don't always come before verbs in questions. You should be sure that you accurately identify the subject before deciding on the proper verb form to use.

items.text: Does John usually eat burgers?; Where are the pieces of this puzzle?

blocks.text: Rule 468
If two subjects are joined by 'and', they typically require a plural verb form.

items.text: The cow and the pig are jumping over the moon.

blocks.text: Rule 469
The verb is singular if the two subjects separated by 'and' refer to the same person or thing.

items.text: Red beans and rice is my mom's favourite dish.

blocks.text: Rule 470
If one of the words each, every, or no comes before the subject, the verb is singular.

items.text: No smoking or drinking is allowed.
Every man and woman is required to check in.

blocks.text: Rule 471

The only time when the object of the preposition factors into the decision of a plural or singular verb form is when noun and pronoun subjects like some, half, none, more, all, etc. are followed by a prepositional phrase. In these sentences, the object of the preposition determines the form of the verb.

items.text: All of the chicken is gone.; All of the chickens are gone.

blocks.text: Rule 472
The singular verb form is usually used for the units of measurement or time.

items.text: Four litres of oil was required to get the car running.

blocks.text: Rule 473

If one subject is singular and one plural and the words are connected by the words – or, nor, neither/nor, either/or, and not only/but also, you use the verb form of the subject that is nearest the verb.

items.text: Either the bears or the lion has escaped from the zoo.
Neither the lion nor the bears have escaped from the zoo.

blocks.text: Rule 474
Indefinite pronouns typically take singular verbs.

items.text: Everybody wants to be loved.

blocks.text: Rule 475
These pronouns (few, many, several, both, all, some) always take the plural form.

items.text: Few were left alive after the flood.

blocks.text: Rule 476
If two infinitives are separated by and, they take the plural form of the verb.

items.text: To walk and to chew gum require great skill.

blocks.text: Rule 477
Titles of books, movies, novels, etc. are treated as singular and take singular verbs.

items.text: The Burbs is a movie starring Tom Hanks.

blocks.text: Rule 478
Compound subjects (two subjects in the same sentence) usually take a plural verb, unless the combination is treated as singular in popular usage or the two subjects refer to the same thing or person.

items.text: Sugar and flour are needed for the recipe.
Neither my dad nor my brothers know how to ski.
Pepperoni and cheese are great on a pizza.
The creator and producer is arriving soon. (both refer to the same person)

blocks.text: Rule 479
Collective nouns can be singular or plural depending on meaning.

items.text: The committee meets here every Thursday. (singular)
The crowd is getting angry. (singular)
The jury has finally reached a decision. (singular)
The majority rules most of the time. (plural)
The staff have gone their separate ways for the holidays. (plural)
The herd is dispersed. (plural)
The class is making a noise. (singular)

blocks.text: Rule 480
In inverted subjects, the subject follows the verb.

items.text: There are seven clean plates in the dining room.
There is a hair in my buttermilk.
Over the rainbow flies a bird.
How are the employees enjoying the new building?
A good gift is a gift card.

blocks.text: Rule 481
If two singular nouns refer to the same person or thing, the verb must be singular.

items.text: The Secretary and Principal is coming. (Here the same person is Secretary as well as Principal)
It is wrong to say – The Secretary and Principal are coming.

blocks.text: Rule 482
Some nouns which are singular in form but plural in meaning, take a plural verb.

items.text: Mathematics is a branch of study in every school.
It is wrong to say – Mathematics are a branch of study in every school.

blocks.text: Rule 483
When the subject of the verb is a Relative pronoun, care should be taken to see that the verb agrees in number and person with the antecedent of the relative pronoun.

items.text: I, who am your friend, will guard your interests.
It is wrong to say – I, who is your friend, will guard your interests.

blocks.text: Rule 484

In sentences that contain the phrase 'one of the...'. (1) In simple form 'one of' or 'one of the', a singular verb is used. (2) In sentences that contain phrases 'one of those who' or 'one of the things that', a plural verb is used. (3) When only precedes 'one of' /'one of those', a singular verb is used.

items.text: One of the books is missing from my cupboard.
He is one of our employees who are always alert.
Ram is the only one of our employees who is always alert.

blocks.text: Rule 485
If the noun in your sentence is plural, the correct choice is what, not how.

items.text: "What exceptional children these are!" is correct.
"How exceptional children these are!" is incorrect.
"What an exceptional child this is!"

blocks.text: What is acceptable with singular nouns as well.
Rule 486

If a sentence begins with any of the following exclamatory words: (i) O that (ii) Would that (iii) If / O if (iv) Were (v) Had (vi) Could (vii) should – use 'I wish' to begin Assertive sentences eliminating the words in (i), (ii) and (iii) and reverting the words in (iv) to (vii) to their positions after their subjects.

items.text: O that I were as rich as Bill Gates. (Exclamatory)
I wish I were as rich as Bill Gates. (Assertive)
Would that I could stand first! (Exclamatory)
I wish I could stand first. (Assertive)
If only I could win the first prize! (Exclamatory)
I wish only I could win the first prize. (Assertive)
Were he as active as I! (Exclamatory)
I wish he were as active as I. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 487

An exclamatory sentence beginning with – 'what', 'such', 'how', 'so' can be transformed into an Assertive sentence according to the following rules: (1) First, put the subject of the sentence followed by its verb, if the sentence has no subject and verb begins the sentence with 'it is' / 'it was'. (2) Secondly, if the aforesaid exclamatory words are followed by nouns, substitute the exclamatory words with 'great' and sometimes as per the sense with – grand, excellent, wonderful, strange, horrid, terrible, shocking, dreaded, etc.

items.text: What a fool he is! (Exclamatory)
