He is a great fool. (Assertive)
What a man Mr. Prakash is! (Exclamatory)
Mr. Prakash is a wonderful man. (Assertive)
What a piece of work man is! (Exclamatory)
Man is a strange / wonderful piece of work. (Assertive)
What an animal the lion is! (Exclamatory)
The lion is a dreaded animal. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 488

If exclamatory sentences begin with the interjections – 'Alas!', 'Ah!', 'Alack!', 'Ah me!', 'Oh dear!', 'Dear me!', etc. begin equivalent assertive sentences with the words – It is sad to think / it is a matter of great sorrow / I am sorry to learn / know; I express my repentance / regret / I repent / regret; I feel great compunction, etc.

items.text: Alas! My friend is no more! (Exclamatory)
It is sad to think that my friend is no more. (Assertive)
Sorry! I got a bit hot. (Exclamatory)
I regret that I got a bit hot. (Assertive)
Oh dear! I have nothing to eat today. (Exclamatory)
You will be sorry to learn that I have nothing to eat today. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 489
If an exclamatory sentence begins with 'To think of', use 'It is strange' to being an assertive equivalent in the following ways:

items.text: (1) To think of my being involved in that crime! (Exclamatory)
It is strange that anybody should think of my being involved in that crime. (Assertive)
(2) To think of my seeing you here! (Exclamatory)
It is strange that I should see you here. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 490
If exclamatory sentences begin with – 'Bravo!', 'Well done', 'Cheers!', etc. use I / We applaud / cry to begin an assertive equivalent in the following ways:

items.text: Bravo! You have performed a great deed. (Exclamatory)
I / We applaud that you have performed a great deed.
Well done! Great victory! (Exclamatory)
We applaud that it's a great victory. (Assertive)
Three cheers for the winning team! (Exclamatory)
We cry three cheers for the winning team. (Assertive)
Or, We applaud the winning team. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 491
If an exclamatory sentence begins with 'Good', use 'I approve' to begin an assertive equivalent in the following way:

items.text: Good! You have behaved well. (Exclamatory)
I approve that you have behaved well. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule continues onto page 164 (outside this batch); examples not printed on page 163.
Rule 492
If an exclamatory sentence begins with 'That', use 'It is surprising' to an assertive equivalent in the following way:

items.text: That you can dare to speak against me! (Exclamatory)
It is surprising that you can dare to speak against me. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 493

If the exclamatory sentences begin with 'Hurrah!', 'Hip! Hip! Hurray', etc., use 'we utter our full throated expressions of joy', 'Our joy is' that; 'We are full of joy that', etc. in the following way:

items.text: Hip! Hip! Hurray! We have won the match. (Exclamatory)
We are full of joy that we have won the match. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 494
If an exclamatory sentence beings with 'Bother', use 'I am annoyed that' / 'I am annoyed with somebody', etc.

items.text: Bother! You have left the key at home. (Exclamatory)
I am annoyed that you have left the key at home. (Assertive)

blocks.text: Rule 495
Places of subject and object are interchanged i.e. the object shifts to the place of subject and the subject shifts to the place of object in passive voice.

items.text: Active voice: I write a letter.
Passive voice: A letter is written by me. — Here, subject (letter) is shifted to the place of object (letter) in and object (letter) is shifted to the place of subject (I) in passive voice.

blocks.text: Rule 496
Sometimes, subject of sentence is not used in passive voice. Subject of sentence can be omitted in passive voice, if without subject it can give enough meaning in passive voice.

items.text: Passive voice: Cloth is sold in yards.

blocks.text: Rule 497

The 3rd form of the verb (past participle) is always used as main verb in sentences of passive voice for all tenses. The base form of verb or present participle will be never used in passive voice. The word 'by' is used before subject in sentences in passive voice.

items.text: Active voice: He sings a song.
Passive voice: A song is sung by him.

blocks.text: Rule 498
The word 'by' is not always used before subject in passive voice. Sometimes, words like – 'with', 'to', etc. may also be used before subject in passive voice.

items.text: Active voice: The water fills the tub.
Passive voice: The tub is filled with water.
Active voice: He knows me.
Passive voice: I am known to him.

blocks.text: Rule 499

The places of subject and object in a sentence are interchanged in passive voice. The 3rd form of verb (past participle) will be used only (as main verb) in passive voice. In Simple Present tense, the auxiliary verb in passive voice is 'am / is / are.'

items.text: Active Voice: He sings a song.
Passive Voice: A song is sung by him.

blocks.text: Rule 500
In Present Continuous tense, the auxiliary verb in the passive voice is 'am being / is being / are being'.

items.text: Active Voice: I am writing a letter.
Passive Voice: A letter is being written by me.

blocks.text: Rule 501
In Present Perfect tense, the auxiliary verb in passive voice is 'has been / have been'.

items.text: Active Voice: She has finished her work.
Passive Voice: Her work has been finished by her.

blocks.text: Rule 502
In Simple Past tense, the auxiliary verb in passive voice is 'was / were'.

items.text: Active Voice: I killed a snake.
Passive Voice: A snake was killed by me.

blocks.text: Rule 503
In Past Continuous tense, the auxiliary verb in passive voice is 'was being / were being'.

items.text: Active Voice: He was driving a car.
Passive Voice: A car was being driven by him.

blocks.text: Rule 504
In Past Perfect tense, the auxiliary verb in the passive voice is 'had been'.

items.text: Active Voice: They had completed the assignment.
Passive Voice: The assignment had been completed by them.

blocks.text: Rule 505
In Simple Future tense, the auxiliary verb in the passive voice is 'will be'.

items.text: Active Voice: She will buy a car.
Passive Voice: A car will be bought by her.

blocks.text: Rule 506
In Future Perfect tense, the auxiliary verb in the passive voice is 'will/ shall have been'.

items.text: Active Voice: You will have started the job.
Passive Voice: The job will have been started by you.

blocks.text: Rule 507

Remember that Present Perfect Continuous tense, Past Perfect Continuous tense, Future Continuous tense, Future Perfect Continuous tense and sentences having intransitive verbs cannot be changed into passive voice.

items.text: It has been raining for two hours.
It had been raining for two hours.
It will be raining.
It will have been raining for two hours.

blocks.text: Rule 508

The Future Perfect Continuous tense is used for stating that something will continue up until a particular event or time in the future. The Future Perfect Continuous tense is composed of two elements: the future perfect of the verb 'to be' (will have been) + the present participle of the main verb (base + ing)
Rule 509

The Past Perfect Continuous tense corresponds to the Present Perfect Continuous tense, but with reference to a time earlier than 'before now'. As with the Present Perfect Continuous tense, we are more interested in the process.

items.text: We had been trying to open the door for five minutes when Jane found her key.
It had been raining hard for several hours and the streets were very wet.
Her friends had been thinking of calling the police when she walked in.
Had you been waiting long before the taxi arrived?
Jane said, "I have been gardening all afternoon." = Jane said she had been gardening all afternoon.
When the police questioned him, John said, "I was working late in the office that night." = When the police questioned him, John told them he had been working late in the office that night.

blocks.text: Remember that this form is also used in the Reported Speech. It is the equivalent of the Past Continuous tense and the Present Perfect Continuous tense in the Direct Speech.
Rule 510

The Past Continuous describes actions or events in a time before now, which began in the past and is still going on at the time of speaking. In other words, it expresses an unfinished or incomplete action in the past.

items.text: The sun was shining and the birds were singing as the elephant came out of the jungle. The other animals were relaxing in the shade of the trees, but the elephant moved very quickly. She was looking for her baby, and she didn't notice the hunter who was watching her through his binoculars. When the shot rang out, she was running towards the river...
I was having a beautiful dream when the alarm clock rang.
I was going to spend the day at the beach but I've decided to get my homework done instead.
I was wondering if you could baby-sit for me tonight.

blocks.text: Past Continuous is used: • Often, for describing the background in a story written in the past tense. • To describe an unfinished action that was interrupted by another event or action. • to express a change of mind • With 'wonder', to make a very polite request.
Rule 511
The intransitive verbs (without objects) which are followed by the same sbjects as they are, these object are called cognate objects.

items.text: I slept a sound sleep. (Active voice)
He dreant a dream. (Active voice)
A sound sleep was slept by me (Passive voice)
A dream was dreamt by him. (Passive voice)

blocks.text: Rule 512
Factitive Object (Object complement) can be changed into passive.

items.text: We considered him honest (Active voice)
He was considered honest by us. (Passive voice)
They elected him President. (Active voice)
He was elected President by them. (Passive voice)

blocks.text: In the first example an arrow points from 'him' to the label 'Factitive object'; in the second an arrow points from 'him' to the label 'Objective complement/Factitive object'.
Rule 513
When the reporting verb is in the past tense, all present tenses in the Direct Speech will change into the corresponding past tenses.

items.text: He said, "I want to go."
He said that he wanted to go. — Here, the simple present will become simple past.

blocks.text: Rule 514
If the reporting verb is in the Present or Future tense (e.g., say, will say), there is no change in the tense of the verb in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: Raja says, "I eat a mango." Raja says that he eats a mango.

blocks.text: Rule 515
The Present tense in the Direct Speech becomes Past tense in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: John said, "I write a letter." John said that he wrote a letter.

blocks.text: Rule 516
The Past tense in the Direct Speech becomes Past Perfect or remains unchanged in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: Ram said, "I brought a pen yesterday." Ram said that he had brought a pen the day before.

blocks.text: Rule 517
The Present Continuous tense in the Direct Speech becomes Past Continuous in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: Peter said, "I am going to church." Peter said that he was going to church.

blocks.text: Rule 518
The Past Continuous tense in the Direct Speech becomes Past Perfect Continuous in the Indirect tense.

items.text: Sachin said, "I was playing cricket." Sachin said that he had been playing cricket.

blocks.text: Rule 519
The Present Perfect tense in the Direct Speech becomes Past Perfect in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: Kamal said, "I have done my homework." Kamal said that he had done his homework.

blocks.text: Rule 520
When the Reporting verb is in the Past tense, the Reported Speech is also in the Past tense.

items.text: They said that they would visit Mumbai next month.
The prisoner thought that he would escape from the prison.

blocks.text: Rule 521
The Present Perfect Continuous tense in the Direct Speech becomes Past Perfect Continuous in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: He said, "I have been reading a novel." He said that he had been reading a novel.

blocks.text: Rule 522
Remember that – 'will' and 'shall' are always changed into 'would' in Indirect Speech.

items.text: He said, "I will go to London tomorrow." He said that he would go to London the next day.

blocks.text: Rule 523
If the Direct Speech contains a Universal Truth, the tense of the Indirect Speech remains unchanged, even if the reporting verb is in the past.

items.text: The teacher said, "The sun rises in the East." The teacher said that the sun rises in the East.

blocks.text: Rule 524
The adverbs of nearness in Direct Speech should be put into those of distance in Indirect Speech.

'now' changes into 'then'; 'here' changes into 'there'; 'here after' changes into 'there after'; 'this' changes into 'that'; 'these' changes into 'those'; 'ago' changes into 'before'; 'thus' changes into 'so'; 'today' changes into 'that day'; 'tonight' changes into 'that night'; 'last night' changes into 'the previous night'; 'yesterday' changes into 'the day before' or 'the previous day'; 'tomorrow' changes into 'the next day' or 'the following day'; 'last week' changes into 'the week before' or 'the previous week'; 'next week' changes into 'the week after' or 'the following week'; 'last month' changes into 'the month before' or the 'the previous month'; 'next month' changes into 'a month after'; 'hither' changes into 'thither'; 'hence' changes into 'thence'.
Rule 525
To change questions, which can be answered in yes or no, into Indirect Speech, word – 'if' or 'whether' is used before the question in Indirect Speech.

items.text: He said to me, "Are you interested?" He asked me if I was interested.
He said to them, "Will you listen to such a man?" He asked them whether they would listen to such a man.

blocks.text: Rule 526
Remember that 'that' is not used between a reporting verb and reported speech as conjunction in Indirect Speech for a question sentence. Question mark is not used in Indirect Speech.

items.text: He said to me, "Do you like music?" He asked me if I liked music. (Not, that I liked music) Or, He asked me whether I liked music.

blocks.text: Rule 527

To change questions into Indirect Speech which cannot be answered in 'Yes' or 'No', the word 'if or 'whether' is not used. The tense of the question is changed according to the rules for change in normal tenses in Indirect Speech but the sentence will not start with the auxiliary verb of the tense. The word 'that' is not used between the reporting verb and reported speech as conjunction and question mark (?) is also not used. Remember that an interrogative sentence is changed into assertive sentence in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: He said to me, "How are you?" He asked me how I was. (Not, how was I)
She said to him, "Why did you come late?" She asked him why he had come late.

blocks.text: Rule 528
When we report commands and requests, the indirect speech is introduced by verbs expressing a command or request, like – ordered, requested, commanded, shouted, etc.

items.text: The master said to the servant, "Go away." The master ordered the servant to go away.
He said to them, "Please wait here till I return." He requested them to wait there till he returned.

blocks.text: Rule 529
When we change Interrogative sentences from Direct to Indirect Speech, the Reporting verb 'told' / 'said' changes into 'asked' / 'enquired of'.

items.text: Ram said to his brother, "When will the train leave?" Ram asked his brother when the train would leave.

blocks.text: Rule 530

Remember that the pronoun (subject) of the reported speech is changed according to the pronoun of the reporting verb or object (person) (first part of sentence). Sometimes the pronoun may not even change as well.
Rule 531

The first person pronoun in the reported speech (i.e. I, we, me, us, mine, or our) is changed according to the pronoun of the reporting verb if the pronoun in the reporting verb is third person pronoun (i.e. he, she, it, they, him, his, her, them or their.)

items.text: He said, "I live in New York." He said that he lived in New York.
They said, "We love our country." They said that they loved their country.

blocks.text: Rule 532
The first person pronoun in the reported speech (i.e. I, we, me, us, mine, or our) is not changed if the pronoun (Subject) of the reporting verb is also the first person pronoun (i.e. I or we.)

items.text: I said, "I write a letter." I said that I wrote a letter.
We said, "We completed our work." We said that we completed our work.

blocks.text: Rule 533
The second person pronoun in the reported speech (i.e. you, yours) is changed according to the person of object of the reporting verb.

items.text: She said to him, "You are intelligent." She said him that he was intelligent.
He said to me, "You are late for the party." He told me that I was late for the party.

blocks.text: Rule 534
The third person pronoun in the reported speech (i.e. he, she, it, they, him, his, her, them or their) is not changed in Indirect Speech.

items.text: They said, "He will come." They said that he would come.
You said, "They are waiting for the bus." You said that they were waiting for the bus.

blocks.text: Rule 535
Remember that the auxiliary verbs should, could, would, ought to and might do not change in the Indirect Speech.
Rule 536
The Indirect Speech is always in the assertive form. In other words, the interrogative sentences in the Direct Speech will change into Assertive sentences in the Indirect Speech.

items.text: Direct: She said to me, "Are you coming with us?" Indirect: She asked me if I was going with them. Or, She asked them if I was coming with them.
Direct: She said to me, "Are you unwell?" Indirect: She asked me if I was unwell.

blocks.text: Rule 537

A quoted wh-question begins with a main clause that mentions the speaker and the verb 'ask', followed by a comma and the exact words of the quote, enclosed in quotation marks. The quoted speech may also be placed before the main clause: "How are you," my friend asks.

items.text: My friend always asks, "Where have you been?"
My friend often asks, "When can you join me for coffee?"
My friend always asks where I have been.
My friend often asks where I can join him for coffee.

blocks.text: A reported wh-question also begins with the main clause, but is followed by the content of the quote as it relates to the speaker in time, person, place and direction, at the moment of speaking. The head of the question clause—who, what, where, why, or how—relates and joins the question to the main clause.
Rule 538
We use 'the' to refer to specific nouns, either singular or plural.

items.text: Please hand me the book that's on the table.
Please hand me all the books that are on the table.

blocks.text: Look at the sentences : Milk is white. The milk of cow is sweet.
Rule 539
'A' and 'An' are used for referring to non-specific nouns.

items.text: Please hand me a book; any book will do.
Please hand me an autobiography; any autobiography will do.

blocks.text: Rule 540
The indefinite articles ('a' and 'an') are used when we are referring to an unspecified thing or quantity. We use them when we don't know (or don't care) which thing we're talking about.

items.text: There once was a sheep. — (Here, we don't know which sheep it was – don't know its name or where it's from, or anything about it – so we can't say the sheep.)

blocks.text: Rule 541
'a' can be used before Mr./Mrs./Miss + surname with a special meaning.

items.text: A Mr. Sinha; A Mir. Sharma
This letter is written by a Ramesh (A stranger by the name Ramesh)

blocks.text: Note : Adding 'a' confirms that the speaker does not know Mr. Sinha or Mir. Sharma. Similarly,
Rule 542
We use 'a' before nouns or adjectives which begin with a consonant, or when 'U' sounds like a 'Y', or 'O' sounds like a 'W'.

items.text: a cat, a university, a young puppy, a one-eyed man

blocks.text: Rule 543
We use 'an' before a word which begins with a vowel sound or a soft 'H' sound.

items.text: an egg, an hour-glass, an antique necklace

blocks.text: Rule 544
Before a non-specific plural noun, 'the' is not used.

items.text: Elephants are intelligent animals.
Cats drink milk.

blocks.text: Rule 545
'The' is used with 'all'. But remember that 'the' should not come before the word 'all'. They may be used separately, or combined into 'all the'.

items.text: It is wrong to say – At the all birthday parties, food and drinks are served to the guests.
This could be written as: at birthday parties…, at all birthday parties…, or at all the birthday parties….
My father asked me to take the all books off the dining room table. (Incorrect)
My father asked me to take all the books off the dining room table. (Correct)

blocks.text: Rule 546
Indefinite article 'an' should be used before any noun – or any adjective modifying the noun – which begins with a vowel or a voiceless 'H'. Some abbreviated form also take 'an' before them.

items.text: an S.D.O., an M.A., an S.P.
He is an ugly man ; He is an honest man.

blocks.text: Rule 547
While using the phrases most of, some of and all of, put the definite article 'the' before the plural noun which is being modified by the phrase.

items.text: I want to clean all of rooms in the house before the guests arrive. (Incorrect)
The phrase 'all of' should be followed by the article 'the'.
I want to clean all of the rooms in the house before the guests arrive. (Correct)
Most of people are careful of their health in winter. (Incorrect)
Most of the people are careful of their health in winter. (Correct)
Some of vegetables are fresh, but some are frozen. (Incorrect)
Some of the vegetables are fresh, but some are frozen. (Correct)

blocks.text: Rule 548
When a preposition is used after a Plural noun, it becomes a definite noun and then a definite article is used before it.
Rule 549
As a pronoun is used for modifying a noun, an article is also used for modifying a noun. Pronouns are words like he, I, we, our, it, her and their. Articles should not be used for modifying pronouns.

items.text: Why are you reading the my book? (Incorrect) — Here, 'the' and 'my' should not be used together. Instead you should write – Why are you reading my book? (Correct)

blocks.text: Rule 550

Uncountable nouns are nouns which are difficult or impossible to count. Uncountable nouns include untouchable things (information, air), things like liquids (milk, water) and other things which can be measured only (coal, sand, wood). Because these things can't be counted, singular articles like 'a' or 'an' should not be used for modifying them. Uncountable nouns can be modified by words like 'some'. Alternately, an uncountable noun can be changed to a countable noun.

items.text: Please give me a water. (Incorrect)
'Water' is an uncountable noun, and should not be used with the indefinite article, 'a'.
Instead, you should write – Please give me some water. (Correct)
Please give me a bottle of water. (Correct)
Please give me an ice. (Incorrect)
Please give me some ice. (Correct)

blocks.text: Rule 551
The indefinite articles, 'a' and 'an' are used for modifying singular nouns. While using a plural noun, these two articles are unnecessary.

items.text: I have a books in my locker. (Incorrect)
I have books in my locker. (Correct)
I have a book in my locker. (Correct)

blocks.text: Rule 552
It is also unnecessary to use an indefinite article if there is an adjective in front of a plural noun.

items.text: When he is in public, he does an embarrassing things. (Incorrect)
When he is in public, he does embarrassing things. (Correct)
When he is in public, he does an embarrassing thing. (Correct)

blocks.text: Rule 553
You should not use an article before the name of a sport.

items.text: I like to play baseball. (Correct)
I like to play a baseball. (Incorrect)

blocks.text: Rule 554

You should not use an article with languages and nationalities (e.g. Chinese, English, French, Spanish, etc.). If you put article 'the' in front of each of these words, it refers to the people of that country

items.text: The Chinese (= people of China)
The English (= people of England)
The French (= people of France)

blocks.text: Rule 555
While referring to a group of people by use of an adjective rather than a noun, you should use 'the'.

items.text: the elderly, the disabled, the employed, the rich, the homeless, the restless, the needy, etc.

blocks.text: Rule 556
Some countries are preceded by 'the', usually if the name is plural, contains an adjective, or includes 'of'.

items.text: the United States, the Republic of Congo, the United Arab Emirates

blocks.text: But there is an exception. You should not put 'the' before Great Britain.
Rule 557
No article is used when two or more nouns are used in pairs or simultaneously.

items.text: from village to village ; face to face ; neck and neck ; from door to door; father and son ; husband and wife; brother and sister; arm in arm; hand to hand

blocks.text: Rule 558
The definite article 'the' is used in front of some geographical names but not in front of others.

1. Do not use 'the' before the names of: most countries or territories (Examples: Canada, China, New Zealand); towns, cities or states (Examples: Mumbai, Paris, California); streets (Examples: Park Street, Lakeview Avenue, Qutub Crescent); lakes (Examples: Dal Lake, Wular Lake, Bear Lake); bays, where the term 'bay' comes after the name; mountains (Examples: Mount Everest, Mount Kilimanjaro); continents (Examples: North America, Africa); islands (Examples: Fiji Islands, Prince Edward Island)
2. Always use 'the' before the names of: rivers, oceans, seas (Examples: the Godavari River, the Indian Ocean, the Mediterranean); bays, where the term bay comes first (Examples: the Bay of Fundy, the Bay of Bengal); gulfs and peninsulas (Examples: the Persian Gulf, the Arabian Peninsula); mountain ranges (Examples: the Himalayas, the Andes); points on the globe (Examples: the Equator, the North Pole); geographical areas (Examples: the Middle East, the South); deserts and forests (Examples: the Gobi Desert, the Black Forest)
3. The names of mountain ranges1 (the Himalayas), rivers (the Brahmaputra), bay (the Bay of Bengal, the Hudson Bay), gulfs (the Persian Gulf), seas (the Black Sea), oceans (the Atlantic Ocean), groups of islands1 (the Andamans), newspapers (The Asian Age), ships (the Titanic), names of holy books2 (the Ramayana), descriptive geographical or significant names (the USA, the Punjab), names of noted public places and important events (the Secretariat3, the PVR cinema, the Siri Fort Auditorium, the Supreme Court, the White House, the Industrial Revolution, the Renaissance and Reformation), trains (the Karnataka Express), planes (the Airbus), spacecraft (the Discovery, the Atlantis).
Exceptions : 1. The is not used before a single mountain or a single island, like: Everest, Madagascar. 2. We say, 'The Ramayana of Valmiki,' but Valmiki's Ramayana. 3. The Secretariat (means the Parliament House), but members of Parliament.
Rule 559
A positive statement is followed by a negative question tag.

items.text: Jack is from Spain, isn't he?
Mary can speak English, can't she?

blocks.text: Rule 560
A negative statement is followed by a positive question tag.

items.text: They aren't funny, are they?
He shouldn't say things like that, should he?

blocks.text: Rule 561
When the verb in the main sentence is in in simple present, we form the question tag with do / does.

items.text: You play the guitar, don't you?
Sania likes tennis, doesn't she?

blocks.text: Rule 562
If the verb is in the simple past, we use 'did'.

items.text: They went to the cinema, didn't they?
She studied in New Zealand, didn't she?

blocks.text: Rule 563
When the statement contains a word with a negative meaning, the question tag needs to be positive.

items.text: He hardly ever speaks, does he?
They rarely eat in restaurants, do they?

blocks.text: Rule 564
If the statement has a modal, it is repeated in the tag.

items.text: Parul can go herself, can't she?
You should get up early, shouldn't you?
You wouldn't do that, would you?
We must help them, mustn't we?

blocks.text: Rule 565
With the Simple Present tense we use 'do', ' does', 'don't', 'doesn't', while with the Simple Past tense, we use 'did', 'didn't'. With the present perfect we use, 'have', 'haven't'.

items.text: They like going to the movie theatre, don't they?
You don't take sugar in tea, do you?
Raju listens to music, doesn't he?
You all watched TV during the night, didn't you?
He didn't read the novel, did he?
Monoj doesn't live here, does he?

blocks.text: Rule 566
Question tags with 'have' and 'do' are often possible after the auxiliary 'have' or 'has'.

items.text: Kumar has two cars, hasn't he? Or doesn't he?
She has a nice kitten, hasn't she? Or doesn't she?
You haven't a house, have you? Or Do you?
They have a garden, haven't they? Or don't they?

blocks.text: Rule 567

If the statement contains words, such as no , no one , nothing , nobody , scarcely , hardly, hardly ever , never , neither , seldom, under no circumstances, etc, it is considered a negative statement and followed by an affirmative tag.

items.text: Julia hardly ever drinks Coke, does she?
Nothing will cure his illness, will it?
He never acts like a gentleman, does he?
She is hardly the right person for the job, is she?
It is no good, is it?

blocks.text: Rule 568
If the subject of the statement is somebody, anybody, nobody, everybody, no one and neither – you use the pronoun 'they' in question tag.

items.text: Somebody entered the garden, didn't they?
Everybody was upset, weren't they?
Nobody objects to the plan, do they?

blocks.text: Rule 569
When the subject of the statement is 'that' or 'this', the pronoun in the tag is 'it'. The pronoun 'they' is for their plural forms — these and those.

items.text: This is an expensive necklace, isn't it?
Those are very naughty children, aren't they?
That wasn't a big surprise, was it?
These weren't yours, were they?

blocks.text: Rule 570
When we use a 'there + be' combination in a sentence, the pronoun in the tag is 'there'.

items.text: There isn't a hotel next to the museum, is there?
There won't be any trouble, will there?
There is a bus to Atlantic City every hour, isn't there?
There weren't any children at school, were there?

blocks.text: Rule 571
When 'let's' is used in a sentence, the question tag used is 'shall we?'

items.text: Let's go to the movie theatre, shall we?
Let's have a party, shall we?
Let's drink tea, shall we?

blocks.text: Rule 572
'Have to' is considered Simple Present and 'had to' is considered Simple Past.

items.text: Your father has to wear glasses, doesn't he?
They don't have to come early, do they?
We had to borrow some money to buy a new house, didn't we?
They didn't have to read the story book, did they?

blocks.text: Rule 573

Some introductory phrases such as 'I am afraid', 'I think', 'I believe', 'I am sure', 'I suspect', 'I suppose' , 'it appears that' , 'it seems that' , 'it looks as if' , 'as far as I remember' , 'as far as I can see', etc. don't affect question tags except for the transfer of negation .

items.text: I suppose you are not serious, are you?
I think my mom returned home, didn't she?
I don't suppose you are serious, are you?
I don't believe you have paid for it yet, have you?
I don't think anyone will volunteer, will they?
It appears that she is enjoying herself, isn't she?

blocks.text: Rule 574
If the subject of the sentence is everything, nothing, something, anything the pronoun in the tag is 'it'.

items.text: Everything is ready, isn't it?; Nothing has the end, has it?
Anything is possible, isn't it?;

blocks.text: Rule 575
After positive imperatives, we use 'will you', 'won't you', 'can you', 'can't you', 'could you', etc .Yet for the negative imperatives we only use 'will you?'

items.text: Open the door, will you / won't you, can you, could you, etc.
Don't play with your toys, will you?

blocks.text: Rule 576
After 'I am', the tag used is 'aren't'.

items.text: I am your father, aren't I?; I am a bit late, aren't I? ;
I am a teacher, aren't I?
